passage:
Week one: Tanuja Ma'am noticed that Rafiq, who usually cracked jokes from the back row, had moved to a front corner and sat with his hood up. When a classmate teased him about his handwriting, he flushed and walked out. She let it go in class and later, privately, said, "You don't have to explain. I'm around if you want to talk."
Week three: Rafiq was eating lunch alone in the library. He answered her greeting with a shrug. She gave him a quiet job sorting books and didn't push.
Week five: The heaviness hadn't lifted. In an essay he wrote, "Everything feels grey and pointless lately." That same afternoon Tanuja gently asked if he would be okay with her talking to his parents and the school counsellor, Mr Thomas. He nodded. The counsellor saw Rafiq before home time, and Tanuja called his mother that evening.

qa.q: Where was Rafiq eating lunch in week three?
qa.a: Alone in the library.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling when she read Rafiq's essay line?
qa.a: She felt concerned, seeing that his sadness had lasted for weeks and was turning into hopelessness.

qa.q: Which choice in week five mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Gently involving his parents and the counsellor that same day, because lasting sadness and hopelessness need more than patience alone.

qa.q: How might Tanuja's quiet approach have felt to Rafiq?
qa.a: Probably safe and respectful; she gave him privacy and small tasks instead of pushing, so he could agree when she asked to involve others.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a cheerful student turn withdrawn and sensitive, offering patience and privacy, then involving family and a counsellor when sadness lasts.

passage: Darshan, you asked how to handle a student who suddenly goes quiet. Let me, Hemant, tell you about Revathi. Years ago she was in my Class Ten, the girl who argued with every poem. That winter she stopped arguing. She flinched when the boys teased her about her new glasses and fidgeted through lessons, tapping her pen till the bench shook. Some teachers called her moody. I gave her time and never questioned her in front of the class. But after some weeks she was still sitting alone at lunch, and one day she told me nothing felt worth trying anymore. That same day I spoke with her mother and walked Revathi to the counsellor's room myself. Years later she wrote to say that walk mattered.

qa.q: What were the boys teasing Revathi about?
qa.a: Her new glasses.

qa.q: What did Hemant feel when Revathi said nothing felt worth trying?
qa.a: Hemant felt worried enough to act that same day, seeing that her sadness had lasted and turned into hopelessness.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Hemant's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Speaking with Revathi's mother and walking her to the counsellor that same day, because weeks of isolation and hopelessness needed more than patience.

qa.q: How might Revathi have experienced being called moody by some teachers?
qa.a: She probably felt misunderstood and more alone, when she actually needed patience and someone to notice her lasting sadness.

grounding: Illustrates a teacher seeing a lively student turn withdrawn and restless, giving patience and privacy, then bringing in family and a counsellor when sadness persists.

passage: With forty-eight students and board exams three weeks away, Anjali Ma'am barely had time to breathe. Still, she noticed Vaibhav. Last term he had been the class clown, first to volunteer for anything. Now he sat by the window, hood up, headphones round his neck. When a classmate joked about his new moustache, he walked out. For two weeks he had eaten lunch alone. Anjali could have put it down to hormones and moved on. Instead, after class, she asked him to help carry copies to the staffroom. On the stairs she said, "You've seemed low for a while. You don't have to explain. But I'm here, and so is Mr Pinto, the counsellor." Vaibhav shrugged. "Everything's just grey, Ma'am. For weeks." That afternoon, with his agreement, she walked him to Mr Pinto's office, and she phoned his mother before evening.

qa.q: How many students were in Anjali's class?
qa.a: Forty-eight.

qa.q: Why did Anjali make time for Vaibhav despite the exam rush?
qa.a: She felt concerned, since his withdrawn mood had lasted weeks and was so different from the cheerful clown she knew.

qa.q: What made Anjali's approach gentle and effective?
qa.a: She spoke privately while carrying copies, didn't demand explanations, and connected him with the counsellor and his mother the same day.

qa.q: What has school been like for Vaibhav?
qa.a: Everything has felt grey for weeks; he is sensitive to teasing and has been eating alone.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a cheerful student turn withdrawn and sensitive to teasing, and gently involving the counsellor and family when the low mood lasts.

passage: Farida Ma'am had taught Neelam in Class 7, when she sang in the corridors and never stopped asking questions. Now, in Class 9 at the Pune municipal school, Neelam jiggled her leg through every lesson, doodled furiously, and flushed scarlet if anyone so much as laughed near her. On Tuesday a boy said she'd grown "long like a giraffe", and she burst into tears and ran out. Farida didn't follow her into the corridor in front of everyone. She handed out a worksheet, waited five minutes, then found Neelam by the water cooler. "Want to be my helper for the science display this week? Just you and me, after school." Neelam nodded. Over three afternoons of cutting chart paper, she talked about growing out of her clothes and feeling "wrong" in her body. Farida mostly listened. She also had a quiet word with the boy's class teacher that same day.

qa.q: What did the boy say about Neelam?
qa.a: That she had grown "long like a giraffe".

qa.q: What was Farida feeling when she chose not to follow Neelam straight away?
qa.a: Farida felt protective and careful, wanting to spare Neelam more embarrassment in front of the class.

qa.q: Why was the science display a wise idea?
qa.a: It gave Neelam privacy, a calm task and time with a trusted adult, so she could talk at her own pace.

qa.q: How does Neelam feel about her body these days?
qa.a: She feels awkward and "wrong" in it, growing out of her clothes and very sensitive to teasing.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a once-cheerful student become restless and sensitive to teasing, and responding with patience and privacy.

passage:
"Akash, stay back a minute?"
"Did I do something, Sir?"
"No. I just noticed you haven't opened your sketchbook in weeks. You used to draw through my whole lecture."
"Don't feel like it."
"And you've been sitting alone at lunch."
"People are annoying."
"Fair, sometimes. How long have you felt like this?"
"Since the holidays, I guess. Everything's boring. I don't even know why."
"That's a long time to feel flat. Sleeping okay?"
"Not really."
"Thanks for telling me. Would you be okay if we talked to Ms Rao, the counsellor, together this afternoon? I'd also like to call your mother today, just to say you've been feeling low."
"You'll tell her everything?"
"Only that you've been low for a while and we want to help. The rest is yours to tell."
"Okay. Can I bring my sketchbook?"
"Please do," said Anirban Sir.

qa.q: What hasn't Akash opened in weeks?
qa.a: His sketchbook.

qa.q: What made Anirban concerned about Akash?
qa.a: Anirban felt concerned because Akash had stopped drawing, was sitting alone, and had felt flat since the holidays.

qa.q: Why is Anirban's plan a good response?
qa.a: Weeks of low mood and poor sleep deserve more than waiting, so he gently brings in the counsellor and Akash's mother the same day while respecting privacy.

qa.q: How does Akash feel about the call home?
qa.a: Akash is wary that everything will be told, but reassured when Anirban says only the low mood will be shared.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a student's withdrawal and boredom over weeks and gently involving the counsellor and family the same day.

passage: Last year Salma was the loudest voice in my Class 9 English period, always first to volunteer. Around February she changed. She sat at the back, flinched at a harmless joke about her handwriting and spent breaks alone in the library. At first I told myself it was teenage moods, so I gave her space and didn't call on her in class. But after three weeks, when she wrote in an essay that 'nothing feels worth trying anymore,' I knew space wasn't enough. I asked her to stay back, just to chat. 'Sangeeta Ma'am, I'm fine,' she said, eyes down. I told her I was glad she was in my class and that I'd noticed she seemed sad. That same afternoon, with the school counsellor, I called her mother. Salma now meets the counsellor every week.

qa.q: Where did Salma spend breaks after February?
qa.a: Alone in the library.

qa.q: What made Sangeeta feel that space wasn't enough?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt worried when Salma wrote that nothing felt worth trying anymore, after weeks of withdrawal.

qa.q: What steps did Sangeeta take?
qa.a: She gently told Salma she'd noticed the sadness, and that same afternoon called Salma's mother together with the school counsellor.

qa.q: What might Salma have felt when Sangeeta Ma'am said she was glad Salma was in the class?
qa.a: Salma may have felt seen and a little relieved, even while saying she was fine.

grounding: A teacher notices a cheerful student turn withdrawn and, when sadness lasts, involves the family and a counsellor the same day.
